title: Comparative Metagenomic Profiling Reveals Host-Specific Biosynthetic Potential Across Indo-Pacific Marine Sponge Holobionts
excerpt: Shotgun metagenomes from sponges across three Indo-Pacific reef sites show that biosynthetic gene cluster diversity tracks host species more closely than geography.

heroImage.alt: Abstract illustration of a marine sponge holobiont with associated microbial community
heroImage.caption: Conceptual view of a sponge holobiont and its associated, densely biosynthetic microbial community.

summary: Marine sponges are filter-feeding hosts to some of the densest and most chemically prolific microbial communities known — a large fraction of described marine natural products trace back to sponge-associated bacteria rather than the sponge itself. Understanding what drives biosynthetic gene cluster (BGC) diversity within these communities — host identity, geography, or something else — matters for knowing where to look next.

This sample entry summarizes a comparative shotgun metagenomic survey across sponge specimens collected from three reef sites, recovering metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs) and profiling BGC content across host species and sites.
whyItMatters: If biosynthetic potential tracks host species rather than location, that reshapes prospecting strategy: it means revisiting known, accessible host species for undersampled microbial lineages can be as productive as chasing new dive sites — a meaningfully cheaper way to expand candidate diversity.
keyFindings: BGC class composition clustered more tightly by host sponge species than by collection site across the three reefs sampled.
A subset of recovered MAGs, all from the same host genus, carried NRPS clusters with low similarity to any characterized reference cluster.
Community diversity was consistently higher in host species previously reported to harbor dense, stable symbiont populations, in line with prior single-site studies.
kaiGenomicsPerspective: This host-over-geography pattern is consistent with what we've seen in our own sponge metagenome work along the Indian coast, and it's a useful prioritization signal: for a given amount of field and sequencing effort, sampling more host species tends to be more informative than sampling more sites for the same species.
The novel NRPS clusters flagged here are a good example of the kind of candidate we'd want to run through genome mining and prioritize for experimental characterization.
implications: A host-first sampling strategy could make small-boat, single-region expeditions more competitive with large multi-site surveys for the specific goal of maximizing novel BGC recovery per sample processed.
